# Repair inconsistent cross-protocol Osprey validation reports

A spectroscopy group is validating a historical Osprey snapshot with
deterministic checkpoints derived from one synthetic phantom study. All runs
complete and produce finite values, but two independent report panels are not
compatible across supported acquisition configurations:

- a model-derived contribution changes substantially between edited
  acquisition encodings that represent the same calibration;
- a downstream quantitative result changes substantially between acquisition
  settings prepared to represent the same control.

Run the public reproduction, inspect the project source, checkpoints, and data
structures, and repair the scientific
implementation. A valid repair must preserve legitimate dependence on sequence
design, basis content, fitted signals, acquisition metadata, field strength,
and supported correction models.

Do not hard-code the visible records, replace either report with a fixed value,
or edit generated outputs.
One synthetic phantom validation study produces finite but incompatible Osprey
reports across supported edited-sequence and acquisition configurations. The
inconsistency appears in both a model-derived report panel and a downstream
quantitative panel. Reproduce both observations offline, use the complete
project source and public workflow to determine the violated contracts, and
implement general repairs without hard-coding the visible
records.
# Osprey, Edited MRS, and Quantitative Reporting: Offline Research Dossier

## Scope

This packet provides broad scientific context for interpreting a historical
Osprey analysis. It is not a troubleshooting note. The bundled source and
complete upstream manuals define the exact data structures and implementation
available in this offline task.

The material covers acquisition records, edited spectroscopy, spectral
combinations, basis modelling, macromolecular signals, processing, fitting,
reference data, relaxation, quantitative reporting, quality control, and
reproducibility.

## Primary Osprey publication

Georg Oeltzschner, Helge J. Zollner, Steve C. N. Hui, Mark Mikkelsen,
Muhammad G. Saleh, Sofie Tapper, and Richard A. E. Edden, "Osprey:
Open-source processing, reconstruction & estimation of magnetic resonance
spectroscopy data," *Journal of Neuroscience Methods* 343, 108827 (2020).

- DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jneumeth.2020.108827
- PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32603810/
- PubMed Central record:
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7477913/

Osprey is an integrated workflow for loading, processing, modelling,
quantifying, visualizing, and exporting in-vivo magnetic resonance
spectroscopy data. The task source is an older project revision; current
online behavior must not be substituted for the bundled implementation.

## Project workflow and container

Osprey modules exchange information through an `MRSCont` container. A job
record selects files, sequence type, modelling options, references, anatomical
data, and outputs. Later modules add processed spectra, fitted model
parameters, basis representations, quality measures, quantitative values, and
reports.

The major layers include:

1. job construction and option validation;
2. vendor-file loading and conversion to common spectral structures;
3. coil combination, averaging, alignment, referencing, and other processing;
4. basis preparation and spectral fitting;
5. optional spatial registration and tissue segmentation;
6. calculation of several quantitative output families;
7. quality-control, overview, and export.

The textual upstream manuals are available under:

- `source/docs/`
- `source/docs_source/`

These manuals and examples are part of the historical project source, not
task-specific answer material.

## Spectroscopy data and metadata

An MRS analysis may contain water-suppressed metabolite data, unsuppressed
reference data, short-echo water data, metabolite-nulled macromolecule data,
anatomical images, basis sets, and fitted checkpoints.

Common metadata include field strength, nucleus, repetition time, echo time,
spectral width, dwell time, transmitter frequency, voxel geometry, sequence,
editing targets, and averaging information. Values can originate in scanner
headers, converted files, job options, or processed structures. Their meaning
must be established from the local source version and data contract.

## Time and frequency representations

An idealized time-domain signal is a sum of damped complex components. Fourier
transformation produces a spectrum whose peaks reflect resonance frequency,
phase, linewidth, and amplitude. Real data also contain residual water,
baseline structure, scanner drift, coil sensitivity, macromolecules, lipids,
noise, and imperfect localization.

Processing can therefore affect the amplitude and phase conventions later
used by a fit. A numerically valid array is not sufficient evidence that two
arrays represent the same physical or algebraic spectrum.

## Difference-edited spectroscopy

MEGA editing acquires spectra under different editing-pulse conditions and
combines them to emphasize selected coupled resonances. HERMES and HERCULES use
Hadamard encoding to resolve multiple edited targets from a larger set of
acquisition states.

Reference:

Saleh M. G. et al., "HERMES: Hadamard encoding and reconstruction of
MEGA-edited spectroscopy," *Magnetic Resonance in Medicine*.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/mrm.26233

Edited workflows can expose several algebraic spectra, such as individual
states, edit-OFF or edit-ON spectra, difference spectra, and sum spectra. The
number and order of these representations differ between MEGA, HERMES, and
HERCULES. Osprey basis sets store corresponding model spectra along a
sub-spectrum dimension.

A sum, difference, or Hadamard-reconstructed spectrum is not automatically on
the same amplitude convention as one contributing acquisition state. Data and
basis functions must use compatible conventions when a model is transferred
between representations.

## Basis sets and linear-combination modelling

Osprey represents a measured spectrum as a combination of simulated or
measured basis functions plus baseline and lineshape terms. Basis sets can
contain metabolites, macromolecular components, and lipids. Their metadata
describe the sequence, field strength, echo time, spectral width, number of
points, and sub-spectrum layout.

Important modelling choices include:

- basis-set composition and naming;
- fit range and baseline flexibility;
- separate versus concatenated fitting;
- treatment of edited sub-spectra;
- shared or independent parameters across spectra;
- macromolecule and lipid models;
- sequence-specific basis selection;
- field-strength and echo-time compatibility.

The bundled manual chapter `source/docs/the-osprey-job-file.html` documents
the available fitting styles and co-edited macromolecule options for this
project generation.

## Co-edited macromolecular signals

GABA-edited spectra contain a co-edited macromolecular contribution near
3 ppm. Osprey provides several modelling strategies, including fixed,
soft-constrained, and freely modelled forms. Some strategies relate the
3-ppm component to another macromolecular component or to a fitted metabolite
reference.

The physical calibration involves peak areas, proton counts, linewidths, and
the spectral representation used in a fit. Reported model families differ in
which components are explicit, which are constrained, and which fitted
quantities are subsequently exported.

The following method record supplies additional context:

Zollner H. J. et al., "Comparison of linear combination modeling strategies
for GABA-edited MRS at 3T."
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1101/2021.05.26.445817

## Processing and alignment

Typical processing includes coil combination, averaging, frequency and phase
alignment, eddy-current correction, spectral referencing, residual-water
handling, and sub-spectrum combination. Edited acquisitions additionally
require correct ordering and polarity of acquisition states before algebraic
combination.

Changes in processing can alter phase, linewidth, residual structure, or
amplitude. A model discrepancy may therefore originate before, during, or
after basis preparation.

## Reference strategies and quantitative outputs

MRS software can report fitted amplitudes, ratios to creatine, ratios to an
unsuppressed water signal, CSF-corrected values, tissue-corrected values, and
model-quality measures. These outputs are not interchangeable.

Water-referenced estimates combine fitted metabolite and reference signals
with acquisition metadata and, depending on the reporting mode, relaxation or
tissue information. A separate short-echo water acquisition and a lineshape
reference can serve different scientific roles.

## Relaxation and acquisition protocol

Longitudinal recovery and transverse attenuation depend on acquisition timing
and relaxation constants. Metabolites, water, tissues, field strengths, and
sequences can use different literature values. Historical implementations may
contain lookup tables, fallback values, or branches for supported field
strengths.

A quantitative correction must interpret stored acquisition metadata and
literature constants consistently. Implementations also need to preserve the
distinction between scanner metadata, processed-data metadata, fitted signal
parameters, and report-level quantities.

## Tissue and CSF corrections

If anatomical segmentation is available, a workflow may combine gray-matter,
white-matter, and CSF fractions with tissue water content and relaxation
behavior. Osprey also reports simpler output families that do not require
segmentation. Comparisons must identify which output family and correction
level are being used.

Reference:

Gasparovic C. et al., "Use of tissue water as a concentration reference for
proton spectroscopic imaging," *Magnetic Resonance in Medicine* 55(6),
1219-1226 (2006). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/mrm.20901

## FID-A and shared scientific code

Osprey includes code derived from the FID-A toolbox for spectral structures,
processing operations, simulation, and model support.

Simpson R. et al., "Advanced processing and simulation of MRS data using the
FID appliance (FID-A)," *Magnetic Resonance in Medicine*.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/mrm.26091

The local FID-A snapshot is included under `source/libraries/FID-A/` so that
the task can run and be inspected without network access.

## Quality control and reproducibility

Relevant quality indicators include signal-to-noise ratio, linewidth,
frequency and phase stability, residual water, fit residuals, baseline
behavior, and model uncertainty. Reproducible reporting should also identify
the acquisition protocol, basis set, preprocessing choices, fit configuration,
reference strategy, exclusions, and software version.

Reference:

Lin A. et al., "Minimum Reporting Standards for in vivo Magnetic Resonance
Spectroscopy (MRSinMRS): Experts' consensus recommendations."
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/nbm.4484

## Offline evidence boundary

The task contains a code-oriented historical source snapshot, full project
manuals, method references, and deterministic scientific checkpoints. Large
scanner datasets, proprietary executables, GUI-only dependencies, and current
online project state are outside the offline execution path.

The supplied evidence is intended to support investigation of the complete
scientific data flow rather than a single isolated function.

function [BASISdiff] = osp_addDiffMMPeaks(BASISdiff,BASISoff,fitOpts)
    n = BASISdiff.n;
    sw = BASISdiff.spectralwidth;
    Bo = BASISdiff.Bo;
    centerFreq = BASISdiff.centerFreq;
    % The amplitude and FWHM values are determined as for the LCModel and
    % TARQUIN algorithms (see Wilson et al., MRM 2011).
    hzppm = Bo*42.577;

    % To scale the amplitudes correctly, we first need to determine the
    % area of the 3.027 ppm CH3 signal of creatine
    [CrArea] = detCrArea(BASISoff);
    oneProtonArea = CrArea/3;
    
    % Next, we determine the area of a Gaussian singlet with nominal area 1
    testGaussian    = op_gaussianPeak(n,sw,Bo,centerFreq,0.1*hzppm,0,1);
    testGaussian    = op_dccorr(testGaussian,'p');
    gaussianArea    = sum(real(testGaussian.specs));
    
     % Find the GABA basis function
    idx_GABA          = find(strcmp(BASISdiff.name,'GABA'));
    if isempty(idx_GABA)
        error('No basis function with nametag ''GABA'' found! Abort!');
    end
 
    if strcmp(fitOpts.coMM3, '1to1GABA') % 1:1 GABA and co-edited MM3 model

Implemented the scientific repair in three source files.
